interpretations: Top 10 accounts overall by order count minus the global average, with the average being total orders divided by the number of accounts that have at least one order. Region is district.A3 of the account's branch district. Ties at rank 10 are cut arbitrarily (LIMIT 10)
Same as above, but ties at the 10th-place difference are all included, so more than 10 rows may be returned
Same as above, but ranking uses RANK or DENSE_RANK on the difference and keeps rank ≤ 10, with ties at any rank kept
Same as above, but only accounts strictly above the average are eligible, so fewer than 10 rows are possible
Same as above, but the region is shown as the district name (district.A2) instead of the region (A3)
Same as above, but the region is shown as both the district name (A2) and the region (A3)
Same as above, but the order count is the number of distinct order_ids per account
Same as above, but the order count is the number of distinct recipients (account_to, or bank_to plus account_to) per account
Same as above, but the order count is the number of distinct payment purposes (k_symbol) per account
Same as above, but the average is computed per region over accounts with orders in that region, and the difference is each account's count minus its own region's average, ranked overall
Same as above, but the average is per region and the top 10 are taken within each region
Same as above, but the average is per district (the account's branch district) rather than global, ranked overall
Same as above, but the average is taken over all accounts in the account table, including those with zero orders
Same as above, but accounts whose district has no matching district row are dropped by an inner join, and the average is computed only over the remaining accounts
Same as above, but accounts with a missing district are kept with a NULL region (left join), and the average includes them

Same as above, but the average is the mean of per-order counts after joining each order to its account and district, so an account's weight in the average depends on its number of orders (rows averaged instead of accounts)
Same as above, but the output is ordered by difference descending, with ties broken by account id ascending
Same as above, but the output is ordered by difference descending, with ties broken arbitrarily
Same as above, but the difference is reported as an absolute value of the distance from the average, so accounts far below the average could also rank
Same as above, but the difference is reported as a ratio or percentage above the average instead of order count minus the average
queries:
SELECT account_id,
       COUNT(*) - (SELECT CAST(COUNT(*) AS REAL) / COUNT(DISTINCT account_id) FROM "order") AS diff_from_avg
FROM "order"
GROUP BY account_id
ORDER BY diff_from_avg DESC
LIMIT 10;
